displayQuote: The truly creative mind in any field is no more than this: a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive

meta.title: Who really said "The truly creative mind in any field is no more than this: a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Pearl S. Buck wrote it — in her 1935 lecture “The Creative Mind at Work.” Her original opens “For the truly creative mind…” with a dash, not a colon.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The truly creative mind in any field is no more than this: a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Pearl S. Buck, from her 1935 University of Chicago lecture “The Creative Mind at Work.” The popular wording trims a “For” and swaps a dash for a colon.

answer.label: Spoken & written by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Buck’s, from her lecture “The Creative Mind at Work,” delivered as the William Vaughn Moody Foundation Lecture at the University of Chicago on 17 January 1935. Her original sentence opens “For the truly creative mind in any field is no more than this — a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive”; the popular version simply drops the leading “For” and swaps the dash for a colon.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: William Vaughn Moody Foundation Lecture, University of Chicago, 17 January 1935
Theodore F. Harris, Pearl S. Buck: A Biography, vol. 2 (1971)

source.excerpt: For the truly creative mind in any field is no more than this — a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive. To him a touch is a blow, a sound is a noise, a misfortune is a tragedy, a joy is an ecstasy, a friend is a lover, a lover is a god, and failure is death. Add to this cruelly delicate organism the overpowering necessity to create — to create — to create — so that without the creating of music or poetry or books or buildings or something of beauty and meaning his very breath is cut off from him.
trail: The full lecture text confirms the line verbatim: “For the truly creative mind in any field is no more than this — a human creature born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive” (lecture PDF).
A footnote to that text dates the speech to 17 January 1935 and notes it was “quoted in its entirety in Pearl S. Buck: A Biography, vol. 2… by Theodore F. Harris… 1971” (source note).
Wikiquote carries the line in its sourced “Quotes” section — not under Misattributed or Disputed — citing the same 1935 Moody Foundation lecture.
source.excerptNote: As it appears in the lecture text. The widely shared version quotes only the first sentence and lightly re-punctuates it — dropping “For” and replacing the dash with a colon.

author.heading: About Pearl S. Buck
author.metaLine: 1892–1973 · American novelist · Pulitzer Prize 1932 · Nobel Prize in Literature 1938
author.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer raised in China, whose novel The Good Earth won the 1932 Pulitzer Prize and helped earn her the 1938 Nobel Prize in Literature — the first American woman to receive it. Beyond fiction she was a prolific essayist and lecturer, and “The Creative Mind at Work” is among her best-known reflections on the artistic temperament.

misattribution.heading: A real quote, lightly re-worded
misattribution.intro: This one is authentic — the “fake quote” risk here isn’t the author but the wording. The version that circulates has been trimmed and re-punctuated from what Buck actually wrote.

items.why: Buck’s sentence opens “For the truly creative mind in any field is no more than this — a human creature…” The popular form drops the leading “For” and replaces the em-dash with a colon, as seen across sites like Goodreads and Quotefancy.

The line is almost always shared with no source at all, detached from the lecture in which Buck develops it — leaving readers unable to check it. Even a dedicated tribute page reproduces it “without attribution details beyond the author’s name.”

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are genuinely Buck’s — from “The Creative Mind at Work,” her 17 January 1935 University of Chicago lecture (full text). Only the punctuation has drifted.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Buck delivered “The Creative Mind at Work” as a lecture on how the artistic mind operates. She divides minds into those that arrange existing material and the smaller, stranger group that must create their own — and it is that second kind she describes as “born abnormally, inhumanly sensitive.”

The line has since been embraced far beyond literary circles — by writers on high sensitivity and creativity — because it frames acute sensitivity not as a weakness but as the price and engine of creative work.
context.pull: To him a touch is a blow, a sound is a noise… a lover is a god, and failure is death.
